title: The sponsor portal
subtitle: Email, lookalike domains, and who is acting on whom
intro: An outside address knew the pledge-desk password by 19:21. Passwords leave a building by email more often than by genius. Pier Nine's mail gateway logs every message as an EMAIL_TRANSACTION. Tonight's inbox was full of sponsor reads, pledge totals and shift notes. Somewhere in it is the message that mattered.
concepts: Regex matches part of a string unless you anchor it
nocase is a word you add, not a setting
A DNS lookup proves a visit, not a password
principal acts; target is acted on
recap: Match part of a string with a regex and switch case off with nocase
Anchor a pattern to the start or the end and say which shape you meant
Read the gateway's action as its decision, not as the truth about a message
Build a baseline from the real sender before judging the lookalike
Pivot from an email link to the DNS lookup that followed it, and list every name a desk asked for
Search the target role when the account was acted on rather than acting

missions.title: Everything about the pledge
missions.beat: Priya remembers 'a sponsor email about the portal, right before we opened'. She does not remember who sent it. Start with the subject line and the word everyone was using tonight.
missions.question: Which messages tonight mention the pledge?

concept.title: Regex matches anywhere unless you say otherwise
concept.text: A regular expression between slashes matches if the pattern appears anywhere in the field. /pledge/ matches 'Pledge Night' and 'Hourly pledge total' alike, once you add nocase. Anchors (^ and $) are how you say 'starts with' or 'ends with'.

explain.meaning: The subject line as the gateway recorded it.
A regex literal. Slashes instead of quotes tell Search to treat this as a pattern.
Comparisons are case-sensitive by default. nocase goes at the end of the condition it applies to.

hints: Run it, then remove nocase and run again. Watch the count change.
Click a row to see from, to, subject and target.url in the full record.
Fifteen messages mention the pledge. Three of them share a subject about a 'sponsor portal' and carry a link.

call.prompt: You remove nocase and the count drops. Why?

options.label: Without nocase, /pledge/ no longer matches subjects that spell it 'Pledge'
Without nocase the regex becomes an exact match, so 'Pledge Night' is no longer a hit
nocase is required for every regex; without it the query silently matches nothing

call.why: nocase only changes case handling. The pattern still matches anywhere in the string; it just stops matching capital letters it was not told about.

missions.clue: Three identical messages at 18:40: to Hal, to Odalys and to the pledge-desk mailbox, subject 'Pledge Night sponsor portal: confirm logo placement before 7 PM', with a login link. The real sponsor wrote at 18:05 from harborlightsponsors.example. This one did not.

logIt.prompt: Log the lure as evidence. Time: 18:40. Source: your query and range. Observation: three identical messages, subject 'Pledge Night sponsor portal: confirm logo placement before 7 PM', to hal.brunner, odalys.reyes and the pledge-desk mailbox, each with a login link; the real sponsor wrote at 18:05 from harborlightsponsors.example. Records: at least one of the three. Where to find it: EMAIL_TRANSACTION, network.email.subject.

missions.caveat: Google's docs warn that a regex starting with .* forces a slow full scan. Anchor patterns when you can.

missions.title: The domain that is almost right
missions.beat: The sponsor's real domain is harborlightsponsors.example. The portal email came from somewhere that merely sounds like a partner. Pull every message from that sending domain.
missions.question: How many messages came from the lookalike domain?

concept.title: Lookalike domains
concept.text: A lookalike domain is not a typo of anything the station uses; it is a name chosen to feel familiar on a busy night. Open one of the three portal messages from the last mission and read network.email.from: the part after the @ is the domain. Matching the end of the sender address with an anchored regex catches every mailbox at that domain.

explain.meaning: The envelope sender the gateway saw.
Backslash-dot means a literal dot. The $ anchors to the end of the string, so it matches the domain, not a mention inside a longer address.

hints: The sender domain is visible in the records you opened in the last mission.
Fill the gap with pier9-partners, keeping the \.example$ anchor after it.

metadata.event_type = "EMAIL_TRANSACTION"
network.email.from = /pier9-partners\.example$/

answer.prompt: How many messages did the lookalike domain send?

call.prompt: The lookalike's messages share one link and a 7 PM deadline. Which detail matters most to an analyst?

options.label: The deadline; urgency twenty minutes before doors open is the classic phishing pressure and enough on its own
The sender domain, which does not match the sponsor the station actually works with, and nothing else matters
Both together; urgency plus an unfamiliar domain justifies checking who followed the link

call.why: Urgency alone is normal on a pledge night. Urgency plus a domain nobody has corresponded with is a phishing pattern worth chasing immediately.

missions.clue: Three messages, one lookalike domain, one link: http://pier9-partners.example/portal/login. A 'portal login' is where someone types a password. Next: did anyone open it?

logIt.prompt: Log a Hypothesis, status open: pier9-partners.example is a lookalike chosen to pass for the sponsor on a busy night, and its portal link is a credential-harvest page. Test next: did any machine on the pier resolve that domain (NETWORK_DNS), and what happened on that machine afterwards?

missions.caveat: The gateway marked these ALLOW. A delivered message is not a safe message; action records the gateway's decision, not the truth.

missions.title: What legitimate looks like
missions.beat: Before you chase the fake, look at the real thing. Harbor Light Sponsors is the station's actual sponsor; its domain is harborlightsponsors.example. Pull every message from that domain and read what a legitimate sponsor email looks like tonight, so the lookalike has something to be compared with.
missions.question: How many messages came from the real sponsor domain, and what do they carry?

concept.title: Baseline first
concept.text: A lookalike only looks like something. Before you can say a message is off, you need the real one beside it: who sends, when, with what subject, and whether it carries a link. The end-anchored sender pattern from the last mission works for any domain; point it at the real one and the baseline falls out of the rows.

hints: Same shape as the lookalike query: the email event type and an end-anchored regex on network.email.from, with the real domain in it.
network.email.from = /harborlightsponsors\.example$/ under the EMAIL_TRANSACTION filter. Escape the dot.

metadata.event_type = "EMAIL_TRANSACTION"
network.email.from = /harborlightsponsors\.example$/

answer.prompt: How many messages did the real sponsor domain send?

call.prompt: Open both real-sponsor records and compare them with a portal message. Which difference is the one worth writing down?

options.label: The real messages arrived earlier in the evening, and attackers prefer to send at the busiest moment, so timing alone separates them
The real messages carry no link and come from a domain the station already corresponds with; the portal messages carry a login link from a domain nobody has mailed before
The real messages went to two people and the portal messages to three, so the wider distribution is what marks the lookalike as a campaign

call.why: Timing and recipient counts vary from night to night. A known sender with no link against an unknown sender with a login link is the difference a gateway rule, and an analyst, can act on.

missions.clue: Two messages, 18:05 and 18:06, from reads@harborlightsponsors.example, subject "Final sponsor read list for Pledge Night", to Tomas and Odalys, target.url blank. Thirty-four minutes later a domain with "partners" in it sends three messages with a login link. The real sponsor never asked anyone to sign in to anything.

logIt.prompt: Write a Harden item: add the station's real partner domains, harborlightsponsors.example among them, to a gateway allowlist, and flag or hold mail from newly seen domains whose names resemble a partner (pier9-partners.example is the example to cite). Answers: your lure evidence. Owner role: IT lead or mail administrator. Urgency: this week.

missions.caveat: Real sponsors do send links. The baseline is specific to this station; build yours from your own mail log before you write a rule that quarantines partners.

missions.title: The one the gateway caught
missions.beat: The mail gateway did stop something tonight. Not the sponsor portal. Pull every message it quarantined and compare what it caught with what it let through.
missions.question: What did the gateway quarantine tonight, and what did it deliver?

concept.title: action is a decision, not a verdict
concept.text: security_result.action on an EMAIL_TRANSACTION is what the gateway did: ALLOW delivered it, QUARANTINE held it, BLOCK dropped it. The gateway decided on reputation and patterns it already knew. A coupon from a bulk mailer trips those; a freshly registered lookalike with a clean link does not. ALLOW on the lure is the gateway's opinion at 18:40, and it was wrong.

explain.meaning: The enum value for held mail. Uppercase, in quotes, like every action.
Open the row and read who sent what the gateway caught. Then compare it with the portal message, which was allowed.

hints: Run it. Then change QUARANTINE to ALLOW and look for the portal messages in the longer table.
Open the quarantined row and read network.email.from, network.email.subject and target.url.
One message: a weekend audio-gear coupon from deals@discount-mailer.example to kenji.mori at 23:10, with a tracking link. The three portal messages were ALLOW.

answer.prompt: What is network.email.from on the quarantined message?

call.prompt: The gateway held a coupon and delivered the sponsor-portal lure. What does that tell you about using action as evidence?

options.label: Action records the gateway's decision with the information it had; a delivered message can still be the one that mattered
The gateway is misconfigured and its log cannot be trusted for this case; the email evidence should be left out of the brief
The coupon was the real threat and the portal message was collateral; quarantine decisions are made on content the analyst cannot see

call.why: A gateway catches what it recognises. The lure was new, well formed and pointed at a clean domain, so it passed. The log is still right about what happened; it is wrong about what mattered.

missions.clue: Caught: a coupon for audio gear, 23:10, bulk mailer, held. Delivered: three messages from pier9-partners.example at 18:40 with a login link. Reputation filters know bulk mailers. They do not know a domain registered for one night.

logIt.prompt: Log the gateway's decisions as evidence. Time: 23:10. Observation: one EMAIL_TRANSACTION tonight carries QUARANTINE, a coupon from deals@discount-mailer.example to kenji.mori; the three portal messages from pier9-partners.example at 18:40 carry ALLOW. Records: the quarantined message (open it, press Add to Casebook). Where to find it: security_result.action on EMAIL_TRANSACTION.

missions.caveat: Gateways map their verdicts to UDM actions differently; some log a quarantine as BLOCK. Check the mapping for your mail source before you count by action.

missions.title: Anchor the start, not the end
missions.beat: Both the real sponsor and the lookalike put the words 'Pledge Night' in their subject lines. Where the words sit is the difference. The real message ends with them; the lure begins with them. Anchor your pattern to the start of the subject and see which messages come back.
missions.question: Which messages have a subject that begins with "Pledge Night"?

concept.title: ^ and $ are positions, not characters
concept.text: ^ matches the start of the string and $ the end. /^Pledge Night/ keeps only subjects that open with the phrase; /Pledge Night$/ keeps only subjects that close with it; /Pledge Night/ keeps both. Same words, three different sets of rows. Anchoring is how you turn "contains" into "is shaped like", and it is also what keeps a pattern fast.

explain.meaning: The caret anchors to the start. "Pledge Night sponsor portal: ..." matches; "Final sponsor read list for Pledge Night" does not.
For comparison: the dollar anchors to the end and returns the real sponsor's two messages instead.
Both senders capitalised the phrase the same way, so the match can stay exact on case.

hints: You want subjects that start with the phrase. The anchor for the start of a string goes before the first character of the pattern.
Fill the gap with ^ so the pattern reads /^Pledge Night/.

metadata.event_type = "EMAIL_TRANSACTION"
network.email.subject = /^Pledge Night/

answer.prompt: What is network.email.from on the first matching message?

call.prompt: Swap the caret for a dollar at the end of the pattern and the table changes to the real sponsor's messages. What does that teach about regex in evidence?

options.label: That anchors are optional decoration; the same two senders would separate just as well with the unanchored pattern and a glance at the sender column
That position carries meaning: where a phrase sits in a subject separated the lure from the real thing, and the pattern should say which you meant
That the dollar anchor is the safer default for subjects, because attackers front-load urgent words and legitimate senders do not

call.why: The unanchored pattern returns five rows and leaves the sorting to you. An anchored pattern states the shape you were looking for, so the result is the evidence and not a pile to sift.

missions.clue: Three subjects begin with "Pledge Night": the three portal messages at 18:40. Two end with it: the real read list at 18:05 and 18:06. The lure borrowed the sponsor's words and put them first, where a busy treasurer reads.

logIt.prompt: Add a Timeline entry. Time: 18:05. Fact: the real sponsor, reads@harborlightsponsors.example, sent "Final sponsor read list for Pledge Night" at 18:05 and 18:06 with no link; at 18:40 pier9-partners.example sent three messages whose subject begins with "Pledge Night" and carries a login link. Evidence ref: the # of your lure evidence.

missions.caveat: Google warns that a pattern beginning with .* forces a slow scan. A leading ^ is the opposite: it lets the engine stop at the first character that does not fit.

missions.title: Who opened the link?
missions.beat: An email link only matters if someone follows it. Following it starts with a DNS lookup for the domain. Find the lookups for the lookalike and see which machine made them.
missions.question: Which workstation looked up the lookalike domain?

concept.title: A lookup proves a visit, not a password
concept.text: DNS tells you a machine asked where a name lives. It does not say a page loaded, and it certainly does not say a form was filled. Evidence stacks: lookup, then connection, then a credential used from somewhere new. Build the stack; do not skip steps.

explain.meaning: DNS queries have their own event type.
The name that was asked about.
You know the exact domain now, so an exact match is faster and cannot over-match.

hints: Use the bare domain from the email link, without http:// or the path.
Replace ___ with pier9-partners.example: no http://, no path, inside the double quotes.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = "pier9-partners.example"

answer.prompt: What is the principal.hostname on the lookup?

call.prompt: One lookup, at 18:52, from a desk signed in as hal.brunner. What do you know, and what do you not?

options.label: Nothing yet; a single DNS record is noise until the same name is asked for again from the same desk
Hal's machine resolved the domain; whether a password was typed is still unproven
Hal typed the pledge-desk password into the fake portal; the lookup at 18:52 is proof enough of that

call.why: The lookup places the visit on Hal's desk at 18:52. The two HTTPS connections that follow it, and the login from outside at 19:21, are what turn a visit into a probable credential theft.

missions.clue: PLEDGE-DESK-02, 18:52, logged in as hal.brunner. Two small HTTPS connections to 203.0.113.44 follow within a minute: a page load and a form post. Thirteen minutes later, someone outside starts guessing the pledge-desk password. At 19:21 they stop guessing.

logIt.prompt: Log the click as evidence. Time: 18:52 to 18:53. Observation: PLEDGE-DESK-02, signed in as hal.brunner, resolved pier9-partners.example at 18:52:30, then made two small HTTPS connections to 203.0.113.44. Records: the DNS lookup and at least one connection. Write what the records show (a resolution and two connections); a password being typed is a hypothesis, not an observation.

missions.caveat: Browsers resolve names from prefetch and cache. In real data one lookup can be a hover, not a click. Corroborate with connections and logins.

missions.title: Every name Hal's desk asked for
missions.beat: PLEDGE-DESK-02 resolved the lookalike at 18:52. What else did that desk look up tonight? List every name it asked DNS for, with a count per name, and separate the ordinary evening from the one lookup that was not.
missions.question: How many different names did PLEDGE-DESK-02 resolve tonight, and which one does not belong?

concept.title: Benign is the background, not the absence of rows
concept.text: A workstation resolves dozens of names in an evening: the weather widget, the CDN, the pledge software, the mail host. Grouping by the name turns that stream into a short list you can read in one pass. The lookalike is one row among eight; it stands out not by count but because nothing else on the pier corresponds with it.

explain.meaning: One row per name asked for.
How many times the desk asked for each.
The routine names float to the top; the one-off lookups sit at the bottom.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
principal.hostname = "PLEDGE-DESK-02"
match:
  ___
outcome:
  $lookups = count(metadata.id)
order:
  $lookups desc
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
principal.hostname = "PLEDGE-DESK-02"
match:
  network.dns.questions.name
outcome:
  $lookups = count(metadata.id)
order:
  $lookups desc
hints: The grouping key is the field that holds the name asked for. You used it in the last mission's filter.
Put network.dns.questions.name under match.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
principal.hostname = "PLEDGE-DESK-02"
match:
  network.dns.questions.name
outcome:
  $lookups = count(metadata.id)
order:
  $lookups desc

answer.prompt: How many rows does the table have (different names)?

call.prompt: Seven of the names are the station's usual services and one is the lookalike, asked for once. How do you tell them apart without a reputation feed?

options.label: By count: a name asked for once is suspicious and names asked for several times are safe, so sort ascending and take the bottom row
By correspondence: the ordinary names match services the station uses and other desks also resolve; the lookalike matches an email nobody expected and no other desk asked for it
You cannot; without a reputation feed every name is equally unknown and the list should be sent to the vendor for classification before it goes in the brief

call.why: Counts mislead both ways: time.sync.example was also asked for once. What separates the lookalike is that it corresponds to the lure and to nothing else on the pier.

missions.clue: Eight names. weather.harborcast.example seven times, the CDN, the pledge software, updates, mail, streaming and the time server once or a few times each, and pier9-partners.example once, at 18:52:30, twelve minutes after the lure arrived. Everything else on the list is also resolved by other desks tonight. That one is not.

logIt.prompt: Log a Gap: DNS shows that PLEDGE-DESK-02 asked for pier9-partners.example once; there is no proxy or browser log, so what page loaded and whether a form was submitted is not visible. Why it matters: the password leaving through the portal is the hypothesis the whole case rests on, and only the connection sizes in chapter 4 corroborate it.

missions.caveat: Real resolvers cache. One lookup can stand for many visits, and a visit can leave no lookup at all if the name was cached from earlier. Treat DNS counts as a floor.

missions.title: Acting on whom
missions.beat: At 19:31 the pledge-desk session on AUTOMATION-01 did something that produced a second login record with a different account in a different field. Find every login where the account being acted on is the playout service account.
missions.question: Who used the svc-playout account tonight, and from where?

concept.title: principal acts; target is acted on
concept.text: UDM roles describe direction. principal.user is who initiated the event. target.user is the account the action was performed on or as. A 'run as' shows up with your account as principal and the other account as target. Searching the wrong role gives a confident, wrong answer.

hints: The account you care about was acted on, so it is in the target role, not principal.
target.user.userid = "svc-playout" plus the USER_LOGIN event type.

metadata.event_type = "USER_LOGIN"
target.user.userid = "svc-playout"

answer.prompt: How many different principal accounts used svc-playout?

call.prompt: The run-as events on AUTOMATION-01 come from the shared account at 19:31 and from dez.okafor at 20:15. What is the right next step?

options.label: Treat both as equally suspicious until each one is proven otherwise, and say so to Odalys before asking anyone anything
Clear the shared account, because the station's own engineer did exactly the same thing on the same machine an hour later
Ask Dez what he did at 20:15 and keep the shared account as the lead, since it followed the outside login

call.why: Context separates them: Dez is the engineer who keeps the PC alive and a restart is in character; chapter 3 checks it in the process log. The pledge-desk use follows an unexplained outside sign-in by ten minutes.

missions.clue: Two actors behind one service account. Dez's restart at 20:15 is routine and he will confirm it. The pledge-desk 'run as' at 19:31 is the first thing the outside session did on the playout PC. Chapter 3 is about what it did next.

logIt.prompt: Log the run-as as evidence. Time: 19:31 to 20:15. Observation: on AUTOMATION-01 the pledge-desk session produced a USER_LOGIN whose target.user.userid is svc-playout at 19:31; dez.okafor produced the same shape at 20:15. Records: both. Confidence high for what the records say; what Dez did is for chapter 3 to check.

missions.caveat: Not every product fills target.user for run-as or impersonation events. In your tenant, confirm which field your identity source uses.
